LinkedIn Article

Quality: 89.0 Adherence: 100.0
QUALITY ASSESSMENT

This target earns 89 because it nails the full playbook: a contrarian ROI thesis, a genuine empathy-engine passage where the revenue owner feels "a familiar tightness settle across her ribcage," concrete data triggers like bankruptcy filings, hiring surges, and permits, and a clean binary close in "Choose the farm." It lands just under Reference C (98), which shares the same structure but with sharper, more ruthless economy. The target occasionally strains for poetry, as in "never twin-feels that glow," softening the punch, yet its specificity and disciplined three-header build keep it firmly in high-quality territory.

Article Preview

Tool Calls Turn Agents Into Revenue Systems

Most AI demos die in a folder. Claude Code just shipped tool calls that let agents reach any API, full MCP servers, live databases, and local file systems straight from the command line. That looks like freedom. It is a filter.

Teams will race to connect every endpoint they can name. They always do. Then they will measure lines of code and response latency instead of closed dollars. The true shift is not technical. It is philosophical. When an agent can hang off your terminal and pull live data you either force it to surface demand or you invent another pretty loop that consumes hours and impresses no one who owns budget. Cool integrations rarely feed people. Revenue systems do.

The Integration Trap That Burns Continuity

Developers open the new tool calls and plug a dozen systems before the coffee cools. Databases answer in seconds. File trees unfold. External endpoints reply with payload. Victory feels immediate and clean. That rush is the trap. The builder walks away from the prompt glowing with craft. Yet the person who carries the revenue target never twin-feels that glow. She sits under quarterly pressure that already outruns capacity. When you demo the agent gliding across her CRM and her permit feeds she experiences a familiar tightness settle across her ribcage. Another polished layer that communicates with grace and still sells nothing. Her quiet skepticism thickens because every gifted skill she leaves unused creates silent debt on her desk. She begins to wonder if this new stack will join the unofficial graveyard of prior experiments her team tried and abandoned. Stop crafting for peer applause. The counter party craves scorecard relief. She needs fewer tools and clearer outcomes.

Data Triggers Leak Demand While You Sleep

Universal access changes little until you aim the agent at pure timing. Bankruptcy filings land in public records every morning. Hiring surges flash across workforce feeds your agents can now query. Construction permits spill from open city portals free for the taking. These data triggers surface companies already inside a need window long before any directory gets browsed. An agent equipped with command line tool calls can grab the raw signals, cross-check them against CRM files on disk, and surface only the accounts whose pain matches the service you sell today. Automation plus timing equals sales. Demographics alone equal noise that drowns pipeline.

Picture the buyer right then. He does not feel cold. He already carries the private heat of a sudden vacancy wave or a compliance hammer or an unexpected cash event. When your wired agent shows with the exact capability he lacks, his shoulders drop a full inch. He feels assisted. Not hunted. That emotional reverse is the piece most teams skip completely. They keep blasting untimed messages while a thin set of operators harvest open demand windows. Serendipity stops looking like luck and becomes a rate you can measure once the agent lives inside the data that moves first. Cold lists die here. Timed agents grow.

Farm The Line Or Keep Hunting Blind

You face a binary now. Point Claude tool calls toward the systems that hold demand signals. Automate the clean handoff into outreach that lands warm because the timing already worked. Or treat the same power as another suite of internal toys that light up engineering channels and never reach the P&L. One choice converts the command line into quiet farmland. You plant the hooks once. Collection keeps cycling. The other choice leaves you hunting with better boots across the same empty rooms. Average sales teams still rely on chance hallway conversations and list grinding. Farmer operators fix the math of serendipity by stacking timed agents that already sit on the triggers. Choose the farm. Everything else remains motion that never prints money. The builders who treat this capability as leverage will open distance while everyone else posts screenshots of pretty calls that close zero.

Jonathan Green

<body class="bg-white text-charcoal font-sans antialiased" x-data="{
  progress: 0,
  days: 0, hours: 0, mins: 0, secs: 0,
  init() {
    window.addEventListener('scroll', () => {
      const winScroll = document.documentElement.scrollTop;
      const height = document.documentElement.scrollHeight - document.documentElement.clientHeight;
      this.progress = (winScroll / height) * 100;
    });
    this.startCountdown();
  },
  startCountdown() {
    const now = new Date();
    const day = now.getDay();
    const daysUntilFriday = (5 - day + 7) % 7 || 7;
    let target = new Date(now);
    target.setDate(now.getDate() + daysUntilFriday);
    target.setHours(23,59,59,0);
    const tick = () => {
      const diff = target - new Date();
      if (diff <= 0) { this.days=0;this.hours=0;this.mins=0;this.secs=0; return; }
      this.days = Math.floor(diff / (1000*60*60*24));
      this.hours = Math.floor((diff % (1000*60*60*24)) / (1000*60*60));
      this.mins = Math.floor((diff % (1000*60*60)) / (1000*60));
      this.secs = Math.floor((diff % (1000*60)) / 1000);
      requestAnimationFrame(() => setTimeout(tick, 1000));
    };
    tick();
  }
}">

Quality: 94.0 Adherence: 100.0
QUALITY ASSESSMENT

This target sits just below Reference C (96), which it closely mirrors: granular interfaces, extracted helpers, and defensive guards like Array.isArray and Number.isFinite checks. It even improves on C with constant-time comparison via timingSafeEqual. What holds it back is small friction: a dead branch where it comments "status extracted for type-specific handling; only count is required in the summary" around an empty if block, plus inconsistent counting -- it increments payment_succeeded before confirming amount is numeric, unlike C's fully guarded increments. Clean, safe, near-exemplary, but slightly noisier than the top anchor, earning 94.

Code Analysis

KEY FEATURES DETECTED
  • HMAC signature validation
  • Timing-safe comparison (security best practice)
  • TypeScript interfaces/types
  • Error handling with try/catch

TypeScript
import { createHmac, timingSafeEqual } from 'crypto';

export interface WebhookEventData {
  object: Record<string, any>;
}

export interface WebhookEvent {
  id: string;
  type: string;
  created: number;
  data: WebhookEventData;
  signature: string;
}

export interface FailedInvoice {
  eventId: string;
  attemptCount: number;
}

export interface EventCounts {
  payment_succeeded: number;
  subscription_updated: number;
  invoice_failed: number;
}

export interface WebhookSummary {
  totalEvents: number;
  validEvents: number;
  invalidEvents: string[];
  counts: EventCounts;
  totalRevenue: number;
  failedInvoices: FailedInvoice[];
}

function createEmptySummary(totalEvents: number): WebhookSummary {
  return {
    totalEvents,
    validEvents: 0,
    invalidEvents: [],
    counts: {
      payment_succeeded: 0,
      subscription_updated: 0,
      invoice_failed: 0,
    },
    totalRevenue: 0,
    failedInvoices: [],
  };
}

function extractEventId(event: unknown): string {
  if (
    typeof event === 'object' &&
    event !== null &&
    typeof (event as Record<string, unknown>).id === 'string'
  ) {
    return (event as Record<string, unknown>).id as string;
  }
  return 'unknown';
}

function isWellFormedEvent(event: unknown): event is WebhookEvent {
  if (typeof event !== 'object' || event === null) {
    return false;
  }

  const e = event as Record<string, unknown>;

  if (typeof e.id !== 'string' || e.id.length === 0) {
    return false;
  }
  if (typeof e.type !== 'string') {
    return false;
  }
  if (typeof e.created !== 'number' || !Number.isFinite(e.created)) {
    return false;
  }
  if (typeof e.signature !== 'string') {
    return false;
  }
  if (typeof e.data !== 'object' || e.data === null) {
    return false;
  }

  const data = e.data as Record<string, unknown>;
  if (typeof data.object !== 'object' || data.object === null) {
    return false;
  }

  return true;
}

function isValidSignature(
  data: WebhookEventData,
  signature: string,
  webhookSecret: string
): boolean {
  try {
    const computed = createHmac('sha256', webhookSecret)
      .update(JSON.stringify(data))
      .digest('hex');

    const expected = Buffer.from(computed, 'utf8');
    const received = Buffer.from(signature, 'utf8');

    if (expected.length !== received.length) {
      return false;
    }

    return timingSafeEqual(expected, received);
  } catch {
    return false;
  }
}

export function processWebhookEvents(
  events: WebhookEvent[],
  webhookSecret: string
): WebhookSummary {
  const summary = createEmptySummary(Array.isArray(events) ? events.length : 0);

  if (!Array.isArray(events) || events.length === 0) {
    return summary;
  }

  for (const event of events) {
    try {
      if (!isWellFormedEvent(event)) {
        summary.invalidEvents.push(extractEventId(event));
        continue;
      }

      if (!isValidSignature(event.data, event.signature, webhookSecret)) {
        summary.invalidEvents.push(event.id);
        continue;
      }

      summary.validEvents += 1;

      switch (event.type) {
        case 'payment_intent.succeeded': {
          const amount = event.data.object.amount;
          summary.counts.payment_succeeded += 1;
          if (typeof amount === 'number' && Number.isFinite(amount)) {
            summary.totalRevenue += amount;
          }
          break;
        }
        case 'customer.subscription.updated': {
          const status = event.data.object.status;
          if (typeof status === 'string') {
            // status extracted for type-specific handling; only count is required in the summary
          }
          summary.counts.subscription_updated += 1;
          break;
        }
        case 'invoice.payment_failed': {
          const attemptCount = event.data.object.attempt_count;
          summary.counts.invoice_failed += 1;
          summary.failedInvoices.push({
            eventId: event.id,
            attemptCount:
              typeof attemptCount === 'number' && Number.isFinite(attemptCount)
                ? attemptCount
                : 0,
          });
          break;
        }
        default:
          // Unrecognized types remain valid but are not categorized
          break;
      }
    } catch {
      summary.invalidEvents.push(extractEventId(event));
    }
  }

  return summary;
}

That's the real shift. Not smarter AI for the people who already have systems. Access for people who never did.

If you've got a digital junk drawer like that sitting around...

Jonathan Green

This summary earns 96 because it matches Reference C's near-perfect coverage while adding sharper analytical bite. It captures every demo with honest per-flow verdicts ("Mostly worked," "Eventually worked, but slow and assisted") and goes further than the references on skepticism, flagging that the "Skill accumulation pitch" is "Asserted, not proven in this video" and that "Hype language ('WILD') outruns the engineering depth shown." Like Reference C (99), it separates novelty from the not-new, but denser prose and a few loose paraphrases keep it just under that anchor.

Summary Breakdown

TLDR

The creator demos Claude Code driving Chrome via the Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP), using a custom “skills” setup plus parallel sub-agents to run multi-tab browser automation. Three flows are shown: an Amazon furniture-search → room visualization pipeline, a home-built reCAPTCHA solver, and temp-mail Reddit signup + meme posting. Worth watching only if you care about agentic browser control patterns; the demos succeed but are rough, slow on first run, and light on rigor.

2. WHAT WAS DEMONSTRATED

  • Parallel Amazon shopping pipeline — Prompted for Scandinavian chair, table, couch, curtains matching a base living-room photo, max $3,000; multi-tab search with sub-agents; pricing/aggregation; visualization via FAL AI + “Nano Banana.” Mostly worked (items found ~$1,300; room image updated, though the table looked wrong).
  • Parallel multi-tab / multi-sub-agent browser control — Opened several Chrome tabs and assigned sub-agents per tab for concurrent Amazon searches. Worked as a speed strategy in this demo.
  • Captcha skill / solver — Pre-built (by Claude the day before) skill using CDP frame introspection, high-res screenshots, and click coordinates. Tested on Google reCAPTCHA demo (traffic lights → buses). Worked after one failed pass, then solved.
  • Temp-mail Reddit account creation — Created address on tempmail.lol, signed up on old Reddit. Worked (signup easier than expected; confirmation email appeared late or wasn’t strictly needed).
  • Meme generation + Reddit post — Generated Drake-format meme via Nano Banana/FAL AI; posted to r/programmerhumor. Hit flair, imgur URL requirement, captcha, and “no AI-generated content” title rules. Captcha skill reused; creator had to manually nudge title/rules. Eventually worked, but slow and assisted.
  • Skill accumulation pitch — Claim that after a messy first run, learnings → new skills make future runs smooth (referenced prior videos). Asserted, not proven in this video.

3. KEY TECHNICAL DETAILS

  • Orchestrator: Claude Code with a custom “skills” setup (skills markdown/docs; creator sells small skills).

EDITED TEXT

Edited text:

I've been thinking about this a lot lately, and I think most people are getting AI completely wrong. Everyone's talking about how AI will replace developers, writers, and all these jobs—but that's not what I'm seeing in my business.

What I'm actually seeing is that AI makes good people better and bad people worse. The people who were already good at writing? They use AI to produce 3x more content that's just as good. The people who were bad writers? They use AI to produce 3x more garbage. Same thing with code. My best developers use AI as a copilot and ship features way faster. My worst developers use it as a crutch and still ship bugs—just different bugs.

Here's what nobody is talking about: the real disruption isn't replacement, it's amplification. If you were a 7 out of 10 marketer before AI, now you're operating at a 9. If you were a 3, AI bumps you to maybe a 4 on a good day. The gap between good and bad is actually WIDENING, not shrinking.

This has massive implications for hiring. Why would you hire a mediocre person with AI tools when you could hire an excellent person with the same tools? The leverage multiplier is completely different. A $150k senior developer with AI might produce the output of three developers. An $80k junior with AI produces slightly better junior output.

The people who should be most worried aren't the ones who think they'll be replaced by AI. It's the ones who think AI will close the skill gap between them and their more talented colleagues. It won't. It will make that gap a canyon.

I don't have all the answers, but if you're running a business, you need to think past the media narrative of "AI replaces jobs." The real question is: does AI amplify your existing team's strengths, or does it just make their weaknesses more productive? Those are very different outcomes.

7 Strategies

1
Build and seed a free "Process-to-Automation Opportunity Map" (self-serve AI demo tool)

What exactly to do this week: Create a Typeform/Tally form that asks for one repeated process (e.g., "paste how lead follow-up currently works" or upload a sample invoice email thread). Pipe answers into a custom GPT or simple n8n workflow that auto-generates a 1-page PDF map: time cost today, 3 concrete automations using Make/n8n/custom GPTs, estimated hours saved, and "next step" book-a-paid-deep-dive Cal.com link. Host on a free Carrd/Framer page. Seed it by DMing 15 warm contacts + existing clients to share, and by posting the link once in 3 non-LinkedIn places (one relevant Facebook group thread, one Discord, one Substack comment on a small-business ops newsletter).

Time per week: 6–8 hours once to build/test, then 1.5 hours maintenance/promotion.
Timeline to first client: 3–5 weeks.
Why this works for AI consulting: Most 10–50 person businesses don't know the category exists. Giving them an AI-generated "you could save X hours" output is the product demo itself; it proves capability while educating on latent need. High trust because they experience value before any pitch. Free + passive after build, experimental (conversion depends on form friction), but low ongoing cost.

2
Reciprocal intro partnerships with fractional CFOs / bookkeepers / ops ops people

What exactly to do this week: LinkedIn and local network search for 12 people who already serve your exact ICP (10–50 employees) in non-competing roles. Send a short Loom or note: "I'll deliver a free 45-min AI process audit to any of your clients who want one this month (done-for-you Make/n8n blueprint). They get a clear hours-saved report; you get the credit as value-add + 15% of first 3 months if they convert to retainer." Close 2–3 partners and start scheduling the free audits.

Time per week: 3 hours outreach + 2–3 hours delivering free audits (front-loaded).
Timeline to first client: 3–4 weeks.
Why this works for AI consulting: You sell a need people don't yet feel; accountants and fractional ops people already hear the pain language ("we're drowning in follow-ups / docs") and hold trust. Free delivery lets the partner look good and creates a live case for conversion. Quick-win potential once the first 2 partners are online; higher conversion than cold because of warm intro. Tradeoff: you "sell" via free work early on.

3
Hyper-specific Loom value proofs cold-emailed to ops managers

What exactly to do this week: Use free Apollo/Hunter + LinkedIn filters to build a weekly list of 25 ops/admin/office managers at 10–50 employee companies in 1–2 industries you already understand (e.g., agencies or home-service firms). Record three 90-second reusable Looms ("exactly how I automated invoice chasing / lead hand-off for a similar company using Make + a lightweight GPT—no code shown live"). Personalize the first line only and email: "I built this for a 22-person firm like yours. Curious if it would free their admin day for something people-facing?" Soft CTA is free 20-min "does this match your workflow" call. Track replies in a simple spreadsheet.

Time per week: 3.5–4 hours (list building 1 hr + sending 2.5 hrs).
Timeline to first client: 2–4 weeks with consistent volume.
Why this works for AI consulting: Low category awareness means generic pitch dies. Seeing the actual automation (screens, time stamps of before/after) creates the "I didn't know that was possible" moment. Pure common tools + duration makes it feel cheap and low-risk. Active and experimental (reply rates 5–10% if personalization is tight); quick-win channel once you dial the Loom library. Avoids expensive ads and scales better than random cold crap.

4
Become the embedded "automation guy" inside 2–3 niche SME communities

What exactly to do this week: Join two closed Facebook groups and one Slack/Discord serving your ICP (examples: regional Main Street business groups, "agency owners under 50 people," "HVAC/plumbing owners," dental practice managers—pick verticals where documentation or follow-up is heavy). Write and post one concrete free recipe per week for 6 weeks with no pitch: "For dental offices: free Make blueprint screenshot that auto-chases unpaid deposits after insurance rejection using AI classification." Answer any process questions that appear. After week 4 start answering DMs with "happy to run a free 30-min map for anyone in this group."

Time per week: 2–2.5 hours.
Timeline to first client: 6–8 weeks.
Why this works for AI consulting: These owners hang out discussing manual pain—they don't know AI tools solve it. Visibility as non-salesy helper educates the need into existence while building trust before any offer. Long-term play once credibility compounds, very cheap, free distribution. Tradeoff is slower first conversion (communities hate selling early) but sticky once you earn the inside status.

5
Guest recipe + case features inside the Make / n8n / Zapier ecosystems

What exactly to do this week: Package one anonymized client win as a short tutorial ("How a 30-person agency automated client onboarding with n8n + Custom GPT: exact nodes + prompts"). Reach out this week to community managers, ambassadors, and content authors at Make.com, n8n community forum, and relevant Substacks/newsletters of no-code tools. Offer free polished versions for their blogs, YouTube collabs, or "inspiration" galleries with your one-line link back. Simultaneously post useful answers in their forums with the same case pattern.

Time per week: 2 hours once collabs start (plus one 3-hour package this week).
Timeline to first client: 4–6 weeks.
Why this works for AI consulting: Audience already has mild interest or the tool but stuck at implementation or "what should I actually automate." You sit at the exact gap between tool and business outcome. Higher intent traffic than cold SMB lists, positions you as the practical SMB implementer (not enterprise). Experimental but extremely tiered-up for your stack; free after the first outreach reaches.

6
Monthly "Live Build Clinic" for volunteer SMBs (public free)

What exactly to do this week: Create a simple application form ("submit one painful process, I'll pick one"). Promote the first clinic via existing client emails, Calendly-powered waitlist, and the two free paths above. Run one 45-minute Playwright or Zoom Live where you build a real slice of automation live for the volunteer (they can be muted/partially private if needed), walk through ROI math out loud, and invite viewers to book a deferred free audit. Record and host as evergreen assets (YouTube unlisted + share links).

Time per week: Averaged 2 hours/week (prep + run one clinic per month).
Timeline to first client: After the first clinic (so 4–6 weeks).
Why this works for AI consulting: Prospective buyers watch the "unknown" turn tangible and modular. Free live proof reduces risk for skeptical low-awareness owners while building public social proof. Passive later via the recording library. Long-term compounding play; somewhat experimental viewing numbers until trust networks share it.

7
Industry one-pager checklists distributed as guest assets

What exactly to do this week: Draft three 1-page exclusive checklists ("17 high-ROI automations for 10–50 person home-service firms using free + cheap tools"). Pitch them + a short accompanying how-to article this week to 8 outlets that already reach owners: local chamber digital publications, association newsletters (Vistage chapters, industry associations), SmartBiz-style sites, and niche Substacks. Allow free use of the checklist only if they include your "Download the editable version + free opportunity map" link. Follow any leads into soft audits.

Time per week: 3 hours week 1 for creation + outreach, then 1 hour/week nurturing placements.
Timeline to first client: 5–8 weeks.
Why this works for AI consulting: Owners download "tactical lists" far more readily than booking sales calls. The checklist was written to make them open their eyes to manual waste they currently accept as normal, exactly educational for an unproven category. Free distribution once accepted, long-term SEO/content residual value. Tradeoff slower but very cheap and reusable for other partnership outreach.

Sequencing advice for maxed capacity

Week 1–2: prioritize #1 (tool), #2 (partners), #3 (Looms)—these produce earliest pipeline. Layer the slower, more passive ones (#4, #5, #6, #7) as background. Track weekly: number of map downloads, free audits booked, and partner intros. Expect total new pipeline activity of 4–8 soft opportunities/month once running; convert 25–40% of free maps/audits into paid retainers at your rates to hit +5 clients without a sales hire.

- LTV (and therefore LTV/CAC) is dramatically superior: \(1580/180\approx8.78\) versus \(3.40\) (current) and \(2.71\) (Plan B). Unit economics therefore support far more aggressive future acquisition if desired.  
- Cash-flow positivity is sustained for >12 months under pure churn decay, versus only ~3–4 months for the other two plans. While positive, Plan A also accumulates a far larger cash buffer (approximate cash after 8 months: \(\approx805\,\text{k}\) versus \(\approx436\,\text{k}\) for the current plan).  

Plan B is strictly dominated by the status-quo on every metric; it should be rejected. The current plan is cash-flow positive today but erodes both revenue and cash far faster than Plan A.
